newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Debt weighs heavy on EMU outlook.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Debt weighs heavy on EMU outlook.

text.p: Europe's mountain of public debt is likely to put one of the Maastricht Treaty's five targets for economic and monetary union (EMU) beyond the reach of most states, a Reuters survey published on Wednesday showed.

The poll of forecasts from 32 economists across Europe showed that only three countries -- Luxembourg, France and Britain -- were expected to meet the guidelines for debt which would make them eligible for planned currency union.
But analysts in the survey said economic statistics were likely to be brushed aside in the political zeal for union.
"The decision to go into EMU at the end of the day will be political, this is one thing the market accepts," said Brian Venables, senior analyst at ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
"The advocates of the EMU criteria tend to be central bankers and technocrats. At the end of the day it's the politicians who make the rules," he said.

The Reuters poll, conducted between February 5 and 10, showed that of the six countries widely held to be the EMU pioneers -- Germany, Austria, France and Benelux, only France and Luxembourg would meet the criteria of having a debt to general domestic product (GDP) ratio of 60 percent or less.
With the notable exception of Belgium, the average forecasts for the other core countries are not far from the target -- Germany is on 62 percent and Austria and the Netherlands are in the 70s.
Even the average forecast for Belgium of 127 percent was improving at a steady rate and could be accepted under the Maastricht Treaty as heading in the right direction.
"The criterion is not that the level be 60 percent but that there be sufficient progress towards 60 percent," said Daniel Gros, economist at the Centre for European Policy Studies in Brussels.

"You cannot bring the debt level down from 120 to 60 percent within two years. The (Maastricht Treaty drafters) knew the level could not come down in time for countries like Belgium or even the Netherlands to join," he said.

Both Belgium and the Netherlands have made heroic efforts to improve their debt-to-GDP ratios and their fortunes were bolstered when they were told last week that gold sales by their central banks had been accepted by European Union statisticians as a legitimate means to cut state debt.
The relative importance of debt as a benchmark for the state of the economy was called into question by some analysts.

The other ground rules for entry include a low budget deficit, low inflation and bond yields and membership of the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM), the structure which limits currency fluctuations.
"As long as you can afford to service your debt, your absolute level is not a problem," said ABN-AMRO's Venables.

Italy, found on average to have a 1997 debt-to-GDP ratio of 123 percent, was the only country wanting to join EMU at birth which was well outside the 60 percent target and making no real progress towards shrinking.
But the political pressure from Rome would probably speak louder than the debt statistics, the analysts said.
Gros, like many of the experts, said the best way forward for EMU would be to accept Italy as a provisional member at the launch of the euro.
"Italy could just elect to join EMU unilaterally. They would take part fully in all the functions, but they would not be part of the decision-making mechanism for one or two years," he said.
"Apart from that they could behave as if they were fully paid-up members."
Italy has made valiant efforts to convince EU leaders that it is economically fit for EMU, warning that the lira would have to devalue if it were left outside currency union.
